extracted.intended_audience: young authors and aspiring writers (especially those preparing periodicals or publishing works)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and stylistic advice for writers about language choices, coinage of terms, presentation of abstruse ideas, and the practicalities and pitfalls of publishing (especially periodicals and subscription-based publication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of symbols to convey highest ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: “An idea, in the highest sense of that word, cannot be conveyed but by a symbol; and, except in geometry, all symbols of necessity involve an apparent contradiction.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an idea is too high for direct statement, it must be expressed symbolically; such symbols often involve apparent contradiction. A philosopher who cannot state the whole truth without producing falsehood or exciting dangerous passions may be constrained to express himself mythically or equivocally. Veracity is measured by the intention to communicate truth, not merely by literal saying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of pedantry
rubrics_metrics.description: “Pedantry consists in the use of words unsuitable to the time, place, and company.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedantry is not merely use of learned language, but inappropriate register. Both the man of the world insisting on only colloquial terms in scientific discourse and the man of letters who converses at the wine-table as if in his library are pedants. Learned ostentation may be more tolerable than contemptuous ignorance; evaluate register relative to audience and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coin new terms when conveying new meanings (example: 'esemplastic')
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge coined 'esemplastic' from Greek (eis en plattein, to shape into one) to convey a new sense and to prevent confusion with existing meanings of 'imagination'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a genuinely new sense must be conveyed, creating a new term aids recollection and prevents confusion with established meanings. Coinage is defensible when it prevents the reader from having to unlearn old meanings and learn altered ones. However, coinage should consider appropriateness to time, place, and audience (to avoid affectation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer new terms over reusing old words with new meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Using old words with newly assigned meanings demands a twofold exertion of thought from the reader — to learn the new definition and to unlearn the habitual meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce new terminology (à la Linnaeus or modern chemical nomenclature) rather than overload ordinary words with new technical senses, because the latter imposes extra cognitive burden and risk of confusion. Where an obsolete but appropriate term can be restored, that may be preferable to coining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminate closely related terms precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples given: adopt 'sensuous' for perception considered as passive; note that 'sensual' has a bad/moral sense; 'sensitive' and 'sensible' convey different meanings. Also reintroduce 'objective' and 'subjective' and distinguish 'reason' and 'understanding'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful, technical discrimination of terms preserves clarity in metaphysical, ethical, or scientific discourse. Re-introducing precise philosophical terms (objective/subjective, intuition as both act and object) can be necessary for brevity and to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid uniting the functions of author and publisher
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge warns against attempting to be both author and publisher: the author who both publishes and sells directly bears extra costs, anxieties, and degrading responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is generally wiser to use the established trade: sell the copyright (or edition rights) for a reasonable sum rather than self-manage publication/distribution. Few authors can expect large remuneration by self-publishing; accepting a modest but certain payment (and ease of mind) is often preferable to the chance of greater gain with allied insults and anxieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not deviate from ordinary trade publishing without strong cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting to publish outside the trade (to avoid taxes or favour certain conveniences like postal delivery) often incurs higher costs, risks, and logistical burdens (e.g., extra paper/printing costs, distribution difficulties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider hidden and up-front costs: buying paper, printing at higher rates, paying postage, and giving away a large share of gross receipts to cover distribution. Unless the current system can be improved without greater inconvenience, practical prudence counsels using trade channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware unreliable subscription lists and canvassing notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Names on subscription lists may be put down without authority, extorted by zealous friends, offered in haste, or intended to be dropped as soon as convenient. An example: an entry for an Earl who had no knowledge of the work and kept many numbers unread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not count subscription names as secure income; check authenticity and be cautious about relying on numbers for financial planning. Personal canvassing can produce inflated or unreliable lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canvass by proxy rather than excessive personal canvassing
rubrics_metrics.description: After initial in-person attempts, Coleridge was advised to carry on the canvass 'by proxy' rather than repeatedly solicit in person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal canvassing is often unrewarding and can be socially awkward; using intermediaries or local supporters to secure subscribers is often more effective and less exhausting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match format, price, and frequency to readership habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge’s periodical plan (every eighth day, thirty-two pages, price four-pence) encountered resistance because many readers 'read little' and were unwilling to commit to frequent, long issues; choices of price/length/frequency affect uptake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning a periodical, consider what your target readers will realistically consume and pay for. Overambitious format/frequency or mismatch with reader habits will reduce subscriptions. Practical examples show readers balking at cost, length, or frequency despite professed ideological support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of controversial content and audience expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing an essay that contradicted subscribers’ expectations (e.g., an essay against fast days) lost Coleridge near five hundred subscribers at once; political or religious provocations can drive away patrons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the likely reactions of your subscribers and patrons before publishing controversial material, especially early in a periodical’s life. If a work relies on a subscription base, alienating core groups can be fatal to continued support; balance conviction with strategic awareness of consequences.
